title: The Cheapest Way to Buy With Special Offers

concept.title: The state is what is still needed; try every offer that fits
body: A shop sells `n` items at normal prices, and it has some *special offers*: a bundle of items for one price. You need an exact list of items (you may not buy more than you need). The cheapest way: the **state** of the search is the list of what you still need. From a state, either buy everything item by item at normal prices, or use one offer that **fits** (it does not give more than you still need), pay its price, and continue with the smaller list of needs.

body.code:
def cheapest(needs):
    key = tuple(needs)
    if key in memo:
        return memo[key]
    best = sum(p * q for p, q in zip(price, needs))          # no offers at all
    for o in range(len(offers)):
        if all(offers[o][i] <= needs[i] for i in range(n)):  # the offer fits
            rest = [needs[i] - offers[o][i] for i in range(n)]
            best = min(best, offer_price[o] + cheapest(rest))
    memo[key] = best
    return best

body: Every offer has at least one item, so the list of needs gets smaller with every offer used, and the recursion ends. Many different orders of using the same offers lead to the **same** list of needs, which is why a memo keyed by the list of needs saves a lot of work. Using an offer twice is allowed if the needs still contain it twice.

statement: A shop sells `n` items; item `i` costs `price[i]` if bought alone. There are `s` special offers; offer `j` gives `qty[j][i]` pieces of each item `i` together for the price `offerPrice[j]`. You need exactly `needs[i]` pieces of each item: you must not buy more than needed. Offers can be used many times. Print the smallest amount of money you have to pay.
inputFormat: The second line has the `n` prices.
The next `s` lines have the `n` quantities of each offer.
The next line has the `s` prices of the offers.
The last line has the `n` needs.
constraints: 0 <= quantity in an offer <= 4, and every offer has at least one piece

examples.note: Buy the offer (3 of item 1 for 5), then 2 pieces of item 2 alone (10): total 15; or buy offer 2 (1 + 2 pieces for 10) and 2 + 0 of item 1 for 4: total 14.

hints: Describe the state by the numbers of pieces still needed.
Without offers you pay the normal prices; try every offer that does not give more than is needed.
Store the best cost for each list of needs.

n = int(input())
price = list(map(int, input().split()))
s = int(input())
qty = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(s)]
offerPrice = list(map(int, input().split()))
needs = list(map(int, input().split()))

# Your code here

explanation: The cost of a list of needs is the minimum of buying all items at normal prices and, for every offer that fits, the offer price plus the cost of the smaller list of needs. A memo keyed by the list of needs stores each result.
solution.complexity: Time O(states * s * n) with at most 5^6 = 15625 states, space O(states).

code.python:
def cheapest(price, qty, offer_price, needs, memo):
    key = tuple(needs)
    if key in memo:
        return memo[key]
    best = sum(p * q for p, q in zip(price, needs))
    for o in range(len(qty)):
        if all(qty[o][i] <= needs[i] for i in range(len(needs))):
            rest = [needs[i] - qty[o][i] for i in range(len(needs))]
            best = min(best, offer_price[o] + cheapest(price, qty, offer_price, rest, memo))
    memo[key] = best
    return best

n = int(input())
price = list(map(int, input().split()))
s = int(input())
qty = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(s)]
offerPrice = list(map(int, input().split()))
needs = list(map(int, input().split()))

print(cheapest(price, qty, offerPrice, needs, {}))
